How to use this atlas

  1. Explore. Use Find your project for three quick questions, or browse all 100 with search and filters.
  2. Choose. Star the projects you want to pursue. My portfolio shows how balanced they are and what is missing.
  3. Act and share. Tick off first steps, print the one-page Decision Brief, or send your picks to a colleague as a file.

In real life A city councillor shortlists five projects before a budget meeting, checks that they cover both prevention and community care, and brings the printed brief to the table.

Why these hundred, and why now

Safer futures are more likely when societies invest at the same time in prevention, resilience, trustworthy institutions, broadly shared capability, ecological stewardship, and ways of learning from mistakes.

The UN Pact for the Future and the Declaration on Future Generations treat today's decisions as carrying duties to people not yet born. The Sendai Framework puts prevention and preparedness at the centre of disaster-risk reduction. WHO's pandemic, One Health and antimicrobial-resistance work treats health security as a cross-sector job, and current AI-safety frameworks put evaluation, monitoring and risk management ahead of raw capability. [S02] [S01] [S04] [S07] [S13]

The highest-ranked ideas lean toward interventions with large, established benefits and limited downside: universal multi-hazard warning, clean air and toxic-exposure reduction, secure-by-design technology, climate adaptation, anticipatory humanitarian action, social protection, public-health preparedness and locally trusted warning networks. More uncertain but potentially very high-leverage areas, such as advanced-AI governance and cross-risk catastrophic-risk institutions, stay in the portfolio as hedges even where near-term feasibility scores are lower. The scores here are transparent planning heuristics, not measured causal effects.

Portfolio principle

Don't fund only the highest scores. A sturdy benevolent-futures strategy looks like a diversified portfolio: mature, scalable prevention alongside exploratory work on emerging risks; central capacity alongside community agency; and no single point of failure in one technology, ideology, institution or forecast. My portfolio shows how balanced your own picks are.

Explore

Find your project

Answer three questions. You'll get the projects that fit who you are, what you care about and the time you have, each with a first step you could take this week.

How this works

  1. Answer honestly. Pick the role you'd act in, not the one you wish you had. Small is fine.
  2. Read the matches. Each result says why it matched, so you can judge it yourself.
  3. Start small. Add one or two to your portfolio and do the first step before adding more.

In real life A parent with a few evenings a month picks "a household or neighbourhood group", "Healing & wellbeing" and "a few hours a month", then starts a Heat/Cold Buddy list for their street.

1Who are you acting as?
2What do you most want to help with? Choose one or two
3How much time and capacity do you have?
How the matching works

Every project gets points: +5 if its lead actor is the one you chose, +2 if it's a closely related actor (for example a household and an individual), +3 for each lens you chose that the project serves, +1 more if that lens is the project's main one, up to +3 for fitting your capacity (a lighter project scores higher when time is short), and +1 if the source material scored it as a priority. The top six are shown. Nothing is hidden: change an answer and the list changes with it.

All 100 projects

Grouped by who would lead the work. Open any card for goals, outcomes, stakeholders, a checklist of first steps, ready-made planning prompts, evidence and related projects.

How to use this page

  1. Narrow it down. Search any word, or filter by actor, effort and lens. "Scored only" shows the 20 priorities.
  2. Open a card. Read it in plain terms first, then the detail. Tick next steps as your team completes them; ticks are saved on this device.
  3. Collect. Tap the star to add a project to your portfolio. Use "Add to Cascade" or "Splice in Forge" to play with ideas.

G01GovernmentHigh effortUnscored

Future Generations Commissioner & Impact Test

Create an independent office empowered to review major laws, budgets and infrastructure for long-term and intergenerational effects, with public…

Learn

In plain terms: A government agency works on long-term governance by trying to represent long-term interests in present decisions.

Create an independent office empowered to review major laws, budgets and infrastructure for long-term and intergenerational effects, with public reporting and evidence access. Pair it with a mandatory future-impact test embedded in ordinary government workflow.

Primary goals
  • Represent long-term interests in present decisions
  • Make intergenerational trade-offs transparent
Expected outcomes
  • Future-impact statements for major decisions
  • More preventive and option-preserving investment
Key stakeholders
  • Legislature
  • Executive agencies
  • Youth advocates
  • Indigenous peoples
  • Auditors
  • Civil society
Concrete next steps

Planning prompts for your team or an AI assistant 5 stages

Paste a stage into an AI assistant, or use it as a discussion question with your team. Change who they're written for with "Prompts written for" above the list.

1PlanningAct as a public-policy programme architect. Build a 12–24 month implementation plan for “Future Generations Commissioner & Impact Test” in [your context]. Start from a measurable baseline; specify scope, owners, budget bands, dependencies, milestones, leading and lagging indicators, a reversible pilot, and explicit scale/stop decision gates.
2Risk and safetyAct as an independent red-team and rights reviewer for “Future Generations Commissioner & Impact Test”. Identify plausible direct harms, second-order effects, misuse, privacy and security failure, perverse incentives, common-mode dependence, excluded groups and failure under crisis conditions. Rank risks by severity and likelihood; propose mitigations, monitoring signals, rollback mechanisms and non-negotiable stop conditions.
3Stakeholder engagementDesign a power- and rights-aware engagement process for “Future Generations Commissioner & Impact Test” involving Legislature, Executive agencies, Youth advocates, Indigenous peoples. Identify rights-holders, frontline groups and people likely to bear costs; specify representation, accessibility, compensation, consent and consultation, grievance and decision rights; then draft the first workshop agenda and invitation.
4Iterative improvementGiven pilot evidence for “Future Generations Commissioner & Impact Test” [paste metrics, incidents, near-misses, costs and qualitative feedback], compare observed results with goals and distributional expectations. Separate signal from noise, list falsified assumptions, recommend the smallest safe changes or experiments, and state the evidence threshold for scaling, pausing or stopping.
5Scale or sunsetWrite the criteria that would justify expanding “Future Generations Commissioner & Impact Test” beyond its pilot scope (budget, staffing, systems it would need to touch), and, separately, the criteria that would justify formally retiring it. Both should exist before you need either.

Start from a measurable baseline; specify scope, owners, budget bands, dependencies, milestones, leading and lagging indicators, a reversible pilot, and explicit scale/stop decision gates.
2Risk and safetyAct as an independent red-team and rights reviewer for “Public-Interest Standards Profile for Beneficial Technology”. Identify plausible direct harms, second-order effects, misuse, privacy and security failure, perverse incentives, common-mode dependence, excluded groups and failure under crisis conditions. Rank risks by severity and likelihood; propose mitigations, monitoring signals, rollback mechanisms and non-negotiable stop conditions.
3Stakeholder engagementDesign a power- and rights-aware engagement process for “Public-Interest Standards Profile for Beneficial Technology” involving Standards bodies, Regulators, Engineers, Civil society. Identify rights-holders, frontline groups and people likely to bear costs; specify representation, accessibility, compensation, consent and consultation, grievance and decision rights; then draft the first workshop agenda and invitation.
4Iterative improvementGiven pilot evidence for “Public-Interest Standards Profile for Beneficial Technology” [paste metrics, incidents, near-misses, costs and qualitative feedback], compare observed results with goals and distributional expectations. Separate signal from noise, list falsified assumptions, recommend the smallest safe changes or experiments, and state the evidence threshold for scaling, pausing or stopping.
5Scale or sunsetWrite the criteria that would justify expanding “Public-Interest Standards Profile for Beneficial Technology” beyond its pilot scope (budget, staffing, systems it would need to touch), and, separately, the criteria that would justify formally retiring it. Both should exist before you need either.

Priority 20 and Score Studio

The source material scored 20 projects on five criteria. Change how much each criterion matters to you and watch the ranking respond. Scores are planning heuristics, not predictions.

How to use Score Studio

  1. Set your weights. Drag a slider to say how much a criterion matters. They don't need to add up; the page converts them to percentages.
  2. Read the movement. Arrows show how far each project moved from its original rank under your weights.
  3. Add your own judgement. Open any of the other 80 projects and use "Score it yourself". Your scores join this table, marked as yours.

In real life A funder that cares most about reaching the most exposed people moves Equity to 40% and sees which projects hold their place.

Projects such as G06 (Advanced-AI Evaluation & Incident Reporting), X01 (International Advanced-AI Evaluation Network), G14 (Strategic Risk-Reduction Diplomacy) and X13 (Cross-Risk Escalation Simulation) remain high-priority hedges despite lower feasibility or controllability scores. Frontier-risk work shouldn't be dropped just because mature public-health or resilience work scores better on present readiness.

How the score is calculated

Each criterion is scored 1 to 5. With the source weights the formula is impact×6 + feasibility×4 + safety×4 + scalability×3 + equity×3, out of 100. In general, score = 100 × Σ(weight × criterion) ÷ (5 × Σ weight), so any set of weights still gives a score out of 100. Ties keep the source order. Only the 20 projects shown were scored in the source material; the atlas never invents scores for the other 80, which is why they say "unscored" unless you score them yourself.

Your portfolio as a night sky

Each project is a star. The direction from the centre shows who leads it (or which lens it serves); the distance shows effort, with quick wins near the middle. Your picks light up and join into a constellation in the order you chose them.

How to read the sky

  1. Hover or focus a star to see the project. Faint threads show other projects that cite the same evidence.
  2. Click or press Enter to add it to your portfolio, or remove it.
  3. Import a colleague's file in Share & collaborate and their picks appear as coloured rings.

In real life A planning team projects the sky on a wall, sees that all their picks sit in the outer "high effort" ring, and adds one quick win from near the centre.

Keyboard: Tab into the sky, use the arrow keys to move to the nearest star in that direction, Enter or Space to add or remove it, Escape to leave. The list view shows the same information as a table.

How to read it honestly: angle and ring are real (actor class or main lens, and effort level). Position within a ring is arbitrary but stable, so the layout doesn't imply dependencies. Brighter stars with rays are the 20 scored priorities. The line joining your stars follows the order you picked them.

    Share and collaborate

    Swap portfolios as files, the way you'd pass a USB stick. There are no accounts and no servers. You decide what leaves your device and what comes in.

    How sharing works

    1. Export. Save your picks as a small file. It's sealed with a fingerprint and a signature, so anyone can tell if it was changed later.
    2. Send it any way you like. Email, chat, a shared drive or a USB stick.
    3. Import theirs. You'll see exactly what's inside before anything is added. Their picks then show as coloured rings in the constellation.

    In real life Three members of a community health board each build a portfolio at home, email their files to the chair, and the chair sees where all three agree before the meeting.

      Data for spreadsheets and research

      Plain files anyone can open. They contain the atlas content only, never your settings or activity.

      For technical readers: the exchange format

      The format separates meaning (validated against a JSON Schema) from integrity (a hash and signature over a canonical form). JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 describes the structure; RFC 8785 defines deterministic JSON canonicalisation (this page uses a simplified sorted-key version of it, not a certified implementation); ECDSA and Ed25519 are standard signature algorithms; IPFS content identifiers and W3C Verifiable Credentials are mature models for stronger, interoperable attestations. [S53] [S51] [S52] [S54] [S56]

      Fields in a portfolio file
      FieldRequiredPurpose
      schema_versionYesSemantic version of this format, currently 1.1.0.
      document_typeYesAlways benevolent-futures-portfolio.
      document_idYesA unique identifier, preferably a UUID URN.
      created_at / updated_atYesRFC 3339 timestamps.
      issuerYesLocal player id, display name and public key.
      projects[]YesYour selected projects in full: goals, outcomes, stakeholders, next steps.
      relationships[]NoDirected edges such as shares_evidence_with, computed from shared citations.
      evidence[]NoThe sources your selected projects cite.
      events[]NoAppend-only log; one selected_for_portfolio event per project.
      extensions.partyNoThe session's people (names, colours, picks) for one-file hand-off.
      extensions.cascadeNoYour most recent Futures Cascade story, if any.
      extensions.forge_draftsNoUp to 20 saved Method Forge drafts, kept separate from the 100 researched projects.
      proofNoSHA-256 hash and, where supported, an ECDSA P-256 signature over the canonical document.

      Versioning, canonicalisation limits and import safety

      Semantic versions: a major bump means readers may not safely interpret the file (this page refuses any schema_version whose major number isn't 1); a minor bump adds backward-compatible fields; a patch fixes documentation only. Canonicalisation here sorts object keys recursively and keeps array order. It matches RFC 8785 for the plain JSON this page produces but hasn't been tested against the full conformance suite, so check before relying on cross-tool verification. The SHA-256 hash and ECDSA P-256 signature use the browser's built-in Web Crypto API. They detect accidental corruption and confirm that a file matches what a given device exported. They say nothing about who is behind that device.

      What import actually enforces: wrong document_type refused; unknown major version refused; files over 2 MB refused; at most five imports a minute; project ids not in this atlas dropped; list lengths capped; every string escaped before display; hash or signature mismatches shown as warnings in the preview, never silently trusted; and nothing merged until you confirm.

      Imagine

      Futures Cascade

      Weave one to four projects into a short story, memo, dialogue, cautionary tale, myth or letter to future generations. It's a thinking tool for workshops and classrooms: every claim in the text comes from a project's own stated goals, and everything else is clearly connective narration.

      How to use the Cascade

      1. Pick ingredients. Add projects with the search box below, or "Add to Cascade" on any card. With none chosen, two are drawn at random.
      2. Choose a form. Mode, year and tone change the shape of the text, not the facts.
      3. Discuss it. Hover or focus an underlined phrase to see which project it came from. The telling number lets anyone recreate the exact same text.

      In real life A teacher generates a "cautionary tale" from two projects and asks students to spot the safeguard that caught the failure in time.

      Ingredients (1 to 4 projects)

        How the combinations are counted, and how to add a mode

        Each mode is a small object with pools of sentence templates and a variantCount(k) function that multiplies the real pool sizes for k ingredients, so the number shown is computed, never typed in. Text is drawn with a seeded random generator, so the same telling number, ingredients and settings always give the same text. To add a mode, add an entry to Cascade.MODES with its pools, a build() that returns segments of {text, sourceId, tip}, and a matching variantCount(k). Segments with a sourceId show as underlined, traceable phrases.

        Imagine

        Method Forge

        Draft a new method of action by combining an actor, a focus area and the traits of up to two existing projects. Every draft is stamped "Generated draft, not scored, not vetted", because that's exactly what it is: a starting point for your team's judgement.

        How to use the Forge

        1. Set the frame. Choose who would lead it and a focus area, typed or picked from the list.
        2. Splice (optional). Add one or two existing projects whose goals and effort level should carry over.
        3. Vet it. Use the five prompts with your team, then save drafts worth keeping. Saved drafts can travel in your portfolio file.

        In real life A hospital resilience lead splices the Heat/Cold Buddy Network with the Near-Miss Learning System and gets a draft for a staff "heat-safety near-miss" log to discuss.

        Projects to splice (optional, up to 2)
          What "genome" and "cross-reference" mean here

          Genome is a project's structured traits: actor, focus area, effort level and, for the 20 scored projects, their five scores. Splicing pulls traits from up to two projects into a new templated draft. It's structured recombination, not biology or machine learning.

          Cross-reference is a plain word-overlap search against the 100 projects and their sources, run on this device. It isn't live research and will miss projects that use different words for the same idea.

          Understand

          Evidence and method

          Where the projects come from, how the 20 priorities were scored, how the six regenerative lenses are assigned, the assumptions behind it all, and a plain-language glossary.

          On this page

          1. Evidence base
          2. How projects are scored
          3. The six regenerative lenses
          4. Related projects and threads
          5. Working assumptions
          6. Glossary

          Evidence base

          The direction of travel rests on primary and official frameworks covering disaster-risk reduction, early warning, health security, antimicrobial resistance, AI governance, cybersecurity, climate science, biodiversity, resource use, open science, education, social protection, deliberative democracy and digital public infrastructure. [S05] [S06] [S19] [S21] [S31] [S57]

          Every project card lists the sources it draws on as S-codes. Sources & conclusion lists all 59, each with the projects that cite it.

          How projects are scored

          The five scoring criteria
          CriterionWeightWhat a 5 meansCaveat
          Potential impact30%Could materially reduce major harms or expand valuable capability across a large population or a long time.High impact is not high certainty.
          Feasibility20%Uses mature methods, realistic governance and plausible financing with a manageable coordination burden.Politics and local conditions can outweigh technical feasibility.
          Safety / risk profile20%Downside is limited, detectable and controllable; the work is reversible with clear stop conditions.A high safety score doesn't mean zero risk.
          Scalability15%Can be replicated, federated or expanded without quickly losing quality.Scaling can destroy trust if local adaptation is ignored.
          Equity15%Benefits reach the most exposed groups, and affected people have real voice, access and recourse.Distribution must be measured, not assumed.

          Score = impact×6 + feasibility×4 + safety×4 + scalability×3 + equity×3, out of 100. Only the 20 projects in the Priority 20 were scored in the source material. The atlas doesn't invent scores for the other 80. You can re-weight the criteria and add your own scores in Score Studio.

          Data integrity check. Recomputing the formula shows that six published totals are one point high (N10, X10, X12, N02, I02 and G02). The atlas keeps the published numbers on the cards, flags the difference, and uses the recomputed values wherever it calculates.

          The six regenerative lenses

          The lenses help you see whether a portfolio heals, restores, builds peace, shares power, compounds learning and prevents harm, rather than leaning on one kind of good. They are computed labels, not research findings. Each lens has a public list of keyword stems. A project's title and focus area count three points per match, its goals and outcomes two, and its description one (each keyword counts at most twice per field). A lens with three or more points is assigned, up to three lenses per project, and the highest-scoring lens is the project's main one. Every project gets at least one.

          Shared power & equitySpreads capability and voice: equity, rights, inclusion, mutual aid, accessibility and community ownership.equity, inclusion, inclusive, rights, participat, community, mutual aid, mutual-aid, social protection, accessib, indigenous, sovereignty, redress, cooperative, commons, timebank, just transition, just-transition, assistive, legal navigation, worker, volunteer, neighbourhood, licens, open innovation, patent, public-benefit, public benefit37

          Prevention & protectionPrevents predictable harm before it happens: early warning, risk governance, safety evaluation and secure systems.early warning, early-warning, risk, resilien, preparedness, cyber, secur, safety, disaster, hazard, emergency, incident, evaluation, biosecur, near-miss, continuity, recall, surveillance, sentinel, anticipatory, catastroph, crisis, safeguard, hygiene, privacy, assurance57

          Keyword rules miss synonyms and can over-match common words. If a label looks wrong to you, trust the project text over the label, and treat the lenses as a prompt for discussion.

          Related projects and evidence threads

          "Related projects" on each card are computed only from facts already in the data: 3 points for each evidence source two projects both cite, 1 point for each shared stakeholder, and 2 points for each shared word in their titles and focus areas. Pairs with at least 4 points qualify and the top three are shown, with the reason. The constellation's faint threads show the simplest version of the same fact: two projects that cite at least one common source.

          Working assumptions

          Budget, geography and timeline are deliberately open-ended. "Low", "medium" and "high" effort are relative to the lead actor. The portfolio assumes lawful, rights-respecting implementation; informed participation where people or communities are directly affected; accessibility; real routes for appeal and correction; Indigenous rights and data sovereignty, including free, prior and informed consent, where relevant; independent review for high-consequence systems; and no unnecessary collection of sensitive data. Community-resilience research generally finds positive links between social capital or community resilience and wellbeing or emergency response, while noting inconsistent measurement and the need for stronger evaluation. [S39]

          Glossary

          Terms of art in plain language. In project cards, terms with a dotted underline open the same definition.

          Early warning
          A way of spotting a coming hazard, such as a flood or heatwave, and telling people in time to act.
          Multi-hazard
          Covering many kinds of danger at once (storms, floods, heat, disease) instead of only one.
          Last mile
          The final step of reaching people, for example getting an official warning to someone with no internet.
          One Health
          The idea that human, animal and environmental health are linked and should be managed together.
          Antimicrobial resistance (AMR)
          When germs change so that medicines such as antibiotics stop working against them.
          Digital public infrastructure
          Shared digital building blocks, such as digital ID, payments or data exchange, run for public benefit.
          Secure by design
          Building technology so it is safe by default, instead of leaving users to fix security problems.
          Anticipatory action
          Releasing help or money before a predicted disaster hits, rather than only after it.
          Social protection
          Public support such as pensions, child benefits or cash transfers that keeps people out of hardship.
          Shock-responsive
          Able to scale up quickly when a crisis such as a disaster or recession hits.
          Citizens' assembly
          A randomly selected group of residents who learn about an issue, discuss it and make recommendations.
          Risk register
          A maintained list of serious risks, who owns each one, and what is being done about it.
          Tabletop exercise
          A practice session where a team talks through how it would respond to a realistic emergency.
          Red team
          An independent group that deliberately looks for weaknesses, harms and ways something could fail.
          Stop condition
          A rule agreed in advance that says when a project must pause or end because of harm or poor results.
          Sunset clause
          A built-in end date that forces a real decision to renew or retire something.
          Pilot
          A small, time-limited trial to learn whether something works before scaling it up.
          Open science
          Making research methods, data and results openly available so others can check and build on them.
          Preregistration
          Publicly recording a study's plan before running it, so results can't be quietly reframed afterwards.
          Reproducibility
          Whether other people can repeat a study and get the same result.
          Data sovereignty
          The right of a people or community, such as an Indigenous Nation, to govern data about them.
          Circular economy
          Keeping materials in use through repair, reuse and recycling instead of make, use and throw away.
          Futures literacy
          The skill of imagining several possible futures and using them to make better decisions today.
          Content provenance
          Information attached to a photo, video or document showing where it came from and how it was edited.
          Mutual aid
          Neighbours and community members organising to meet each other's needs directly.
          Interoperability
          When different systems can work together and exchange information smoothly.
          Climate adaptation
          Changes that help people and places cope with the effects of climate change, such as heat or flooding.
          Biosecurity
          Measures that prevent the misuse, theft or accidental release of dangerous biological materials.
          Option value
          The benefit of keeping future choices open instead of locking in a decision too early.
          Lock-in
          When a decision, such as long-lived infrastructure, becomes very hard or costly to change later.
          Common-mode failure
          When many safeguards fail at once because they all depend on the same thing.
          Near-miss
          Something that almost went wrong. Recording near-misses lets a team fix problems before they cause harm.
          Wastewater surveillance
          Testing sewage for signs of disease, which can show an outbreak early without testing individuals.
          Just transition
          Moving to a low-carbon economy in a way that protects workers and communities who depend on older industries.
          Safety case
          A structured, evidence-backed argument that a system is acceptably safe for a specific use.
          Hash
          A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents. Any change to the file changes the fingerprint.
          Digital signature
          A mathematical seal showing that a file hasn't changed since a particular device signed it.

          Understand

          Sources and conclusion

          A starting sequence, the limits of this atlas, how it may be reused, and every source it cites.

          On this page

          1. A starting sequence
          2. Open questions and limitations
          3. Attribution and licensing
          4. All 59 sources

          A starting sequence

          A safer future is unlikely to come from one breakthrough. The more defensible strategy is a mesh of benevolent capabilities: institutions that think beyond short budget cycles; governments that prevent predictable harm; schools that teach uncertainty and verification; businesses that build safety in; communities with real mutual-aid capacity; individuals with lasting civic habits; and consortia that make evidence and safeguards work together.

          In practice: choose a balanced portfolio of three to seven projects; set baselines and rights and safety limits before choosing solutions; start with reversible pilots; write down success, equity and stop conditions in advance; involve affected people in governance; publish evidence and near-misses; and scale only after independent review. For a first diversified portfolio, G03 or N01 covers acute resilience, G10 or N10 preventive health, E01 long-term capability, PV02 or G07 digital infrastructure, C01 local social resilience, and G06 or X01 a frontier-risk hedge.

          Open questions and limitations

          The ranking is global and can't encode local political legitimacy, institutional capacity, hazard exposure, budgets, culture or opportunity cost. Several proposals, especially on advanced AI, new data institutions, long-horizon governance and cross-risk coordination, have thinner implementation evidence than mature work in public health, cybersecurity or disaster preparedness. Recompute the scores with local evidence and stakeholder weighting before committing resources. This atlas avoids operational biological, cyber-offensive, weapons or other dual-use instructions; projects in nearby areas are framed around prevention, governance, monitoring and resilience.

          About

          About and settings

          The Zero Harm covenant, your display settings, exactly what this page stores on your device, and how to back it up or erase it.

          On this page

          1. Zero Harm & Anti-Coercion
          2. Display settings
          3. Your data
          4. Accessibility
          5. Keyboard shortcuts
          6. Version and citation

          Zero Harm & Anti-Coercion

          Zero Harm. Nothing here is designed to surveil, profile, manipulate, deceive, sexualise or coerce anyone, including children. There are no trackers, no advertising, no accounts and no network requests of any kind.

          Anti-Coercion. Every feature that could in theory be turned against the people it serves is deliberately narrowed. Exports need an explicit click. Imports are size-capped, escaped and previewed, and nothing is merged until you agree. Usage counters are off unless you switch them on, and they never leave this device. Generated text is always labelled as generated, never presented as a forecast. Gamification counts exploration, never rank or rivalry between people.

          Peace-aligned by design. The atlas avoids operational detail that could be misused, and frames work in sensitive areas around prevention, governance, monitoring and repair.

          Theme

          "How to use" guides

          Your data

          Everything you do here is saved only in this browser, using checking…. Open tabs of this page stay in sync with each other. Nothing is sent anywhere.

          Optional usage counters

          Accessibility

          This page aims for WCAG 2.2 level AA. Text colours are checked for at least 4.5:1 contrast in both themes; every control works with a keyboard and shows a visible focus ring; icon-only buttons have labels; moving content can be paused; and motion follows your device's "reduce motion" setting unless you choose otherwise above. The body typeface, Atkinson Hyperlegible Next, was designed for readers with low vision. Charts have table views, and the constellation has a keyboard mode and a list view. Known limitation: the constellation's evidence threads are only visible on screen; the same facts appear as "Related projects" on each card. This is a static file with no backend, so there's no contact form; if you hit a barrier, note the project code and the problem and pass it to whoever shared this atlas with you.
